t: Why You Shouldn’t Stay Late After School
q: There are those rare teachers, perhaps one or two at every school site, who pride themselves with how late they stay after school.
But the truth is, for most teachers, staying late is a mistake.
After a long day of teaching, a long day on your feet talking, making decisions, and managing your classroom, your mind won’t be nearly as sharp and clear as it was when you arrived in the morning.
Denying this need day after day will tear you up inside and cause a great amount of stress.
To be the best teacher you can be for your students, to have patience, calmness, and likability, to have spot-on classroom management and a passion for teaching, you must get away from it.
If you can carve out an extra fifteen minutes, just fifteen minutes, you'll save yourself a half hour in the afternoon.

t: How To Handle Sleepy, Unprepared, And Unmotivated Students otivated-students/
q: They enter your classroom bleary eyed. Some have bed-head and pillow lines etched on their faces.
The truth is, regardless of how strongly you harp on coming to school prepared, you can’t always count on students to arrive with the mental and physical sharpness needed for optimal learning.
The key to this strategy is not giving your students the opportunity to sleepwalk into your classroom.
Make sure your students have immediate and multiple responsibilities upon entering your classroom—prepping homework, hanging backpacks, organizing materials, checking mailboxes.
The relationship between exercise and mental performance is a close one; it pays to use it to your advantage.
By starting the day task focused and brisk moving, you’re grooving an association of attentiveness, independence, and responsibility with the ringing of the morning bell.
x: Linsin acknowledges that students often arrive at school mentally and physically unready for learning, and argues teachers must proactively counteract this rather than leave it to chance.
Students often arrive physically and mentally unready to learn.
Meet students outside the classroom before the bell rather than letting them 'sleepwalk' directly into the room.
Move students immediately into purposeful morning responsibilities—unpacking, organizing materials, checking mailboxes—that have been previously taught and practiced.
If students remain sluggish, brief physical activity like jumping jacks can boost alertness, since exercise and mental performance are closely linked.
The piece frames this brisk, purposeful morning sequence as 'flipping a switch' that associates the school bell with focus and energy rather than drowsiness.

t: A Non-Freaked Out, Focused Approach to the Common Core — Part 3 — Close Reading
q: As with most hyped stuff, there's a lot of misinformation out there about close reading, a lot of “beating texts with a hose” just for the sake of doing it, stuff that confuses kids and makes reading weird and unnatural.

If you came into our classes and asked our students what close reading is, what they'd probably describe is something that can be boiled down to this: the careful interpretation of a text wherein readers pay close attention to the way ideas unfold as they read. Often, this involves annotating texts for the sake of slowing ourselves down and recording our thinking so that we can do cool stuff with what you read.

We ask students to closely read because we ask them to read texts that are appropriately complex for their grade level, and that means that many of our students are going to struggle. When Erica and I started college, we began close reading intuitively, but we called it something like “write in the book so you don't fail.

Kids understand that we don't close read everything; we don't close read recreational reading, for example. Close reading everything would kill a love for reading, and “book love” is something that we try to cultivate in our students through other aspects of our curriculum.

Essentially, close reading is a specific skill that we believe will help our kids practice understanding and using complex texts for diverse purposes. In other words, we provide students with repeated close reading opportunities so that they can flourish in the long-term, no matter what path they take.

Close reading in isolation makes no sense at all. After all, at no point when we naturally learned to close read did we simply do it “because.” We did it to help us pwn intellectual, text-based tasks like discussion and argument, both written and spoken.
x: He stresses that not everything should be close read, since doing so would kill a love of reading.
He defines it plainly as careful interpretation of a text, attending to how ideas unfold, usually with annotation to slow the reader down.
Stuart defends close reading as a practical survival skill for complex texts, the same thing he and Beaton did in college under the name 'write in the book so you don't fail.'.
He warns that close reading everything, including recreational reading, would kill the 'book love' teachers cultivate elsewhere in the curriculum.

t: How To Handle Students Who Complain And Talk Back When Sent To Time-Out talk-back-when-sent-to-time-out/
q: Karla, in response, is furious. She glares at you and yells, “But I didn’t do anything wrong! This is so unfair!

Now for most teachers, their first inclination is to follow Karla to time-out to either try to talk things out, explain how she should respond, or cut loose with a well-deserved, how-dare-you lecture.
Any effort to discuss with Karla her angry reaction to being placed in time-out will only cause an increase in friction between you.
Attempting to talk with her, or “put her in her place,” will interfere with the purpose of the consequence—which is to hold her accountable for misbehavior.
You must give your students an opportunity to think for themselves, to accept the consequences for their behavior and learn from them on their own terms—even if that means a show of anger.
If a student like Karla reacts angrily or immaturely to being sent to time-out, so be it. It’s not your issue.

t: A Non-Freaked Out, Focused Approach to the Common Core — Part 2 — Complex Texts
q: If you've been hearing “complex text” phraseology thrown around like crazy lately, it's because one of the central shifts that the Common Core promotes is the idea that, instead of only giving students books that are within their zone of proximal development (“just right” books), we should be asking students to read texts that are appropriately complex for their age.

The most common (and powerful) critique of the extended whole-class text approach that I'm using is this: most students just won't (or just can't) read grade-level complex texts on their own. Therefore, it's a huge waste of time to assign anything more than an article-length complex text.

So, keeping that 46% in mind, I currently consider 70% the “win threshold.” As you can see above, Things Fall Apart — the first book I tracked — was pretty much a fail. However, we saw quite an increase in completion with our next extended complex text, All Quiet on the Western Front. If we can keep those numbers up during the remaining months of school, I'll be pumped. And I know that, even if students didn't finish the assigned reading, due to the way I've structured class, all are reading, writing about, and discussing large portions of it.

Start slow: More than once, I've felt pressure to cover a book quickly, and that pressure has led me to assign just as many pages at the beginning of a reading unit as I do at the end. This doesn't work well; many students quit.

And indeed, if it's true that most students won't read what's assigned, it is a wasted assignment for most students. So, seeking to determine what percentage of my students were reading the assigned texts, I began tracking the percentage who had completed the previous day's reading assignment (see image below).

While I do use choice reading (most heavily in the first trimester), I don't choose to go “all in” on it. When I asked Penny for her reasoning in doing so, she honestly answered that she tries to weigh out what is gained and what is lost. I couldn't agree with her more in that kind of thinking; there is no “silver bullet” in education.

My goal as a world history teacher is to build a fence in my student's brains. The fence itself represents a chronological framework of world history; the fenceposts represent deeper learning experiences (e.g., digging into some source documents or articles; simulating socialism and capitalism; reading Escape from Camp 14 or Julius Caesar).
x: Stuart lays out how he meets the Common Core's text-complexity shift by having whole classes read shared, extended, grade-level complex texts rather than relying mainly on 'just right' choice books.

Confronting the strongest objection, that most students simply won't read assigned complex texts, he started tracking the daily percentage of students who completed the reading against a 70% 'win threshold'.
